sources.title: Meta made a Tamagotchi-like wearable for its Muse AI agent - TechCrunch
passages: Appropriate for what it offers, the gadget has a quasi-Tamagotchi feel to it — a lightweight, personality-filled device designed to keep users always connected to Meta’s software.
It also feels like a relatively low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses.
The Muse agent, which is now embodied by a cute digital avatar known within the company as Jolly, lives inside the palm-sized totem that users can carry in their pockets or attach to a keychain.

“We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s keynote. “You just go ahead and tap here in the fingerprint sensor in the corner, and you can start talking without having to unlock a phone or open an app.”

extraction.body: The AI amulet has become a bit of a cliché in the tech industry — devices like Friend have turned the idea of physical AI into little more than an exercise in eye-rolling for many consumers. But that hasn’t stopped Meta from jumping into the arena with its own AI wearable, called Muse Charm, which is designed to give consumers another way to stay connected to its recently launched, and already popular, personal AI agent, Muse. The device, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed in a “one more thing” moment during the company’s annual Connect event, isn’t ready to ship just yet. Zuckerberg said his team had to “finalize laying out the components” and promised the devices would be “ready to ship in time for the holidays in December.” The Muse agent, which is now embodied by a cute digital avatar known within the company as Jolly, lives inside the palm-sized totem that users can carry in their pockets or attach to a keychain. The device comes with a tiny screen that displays the avatar representing the agent. Users can talk to the device, which can then presumably carry out tasks on their behalf. “We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s keynote. “You just go ahead and tap here in the fingerprint sensor in the corner, and you can start talking without having to unlock a phone or open an app.” Zuckerberg added: “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show what’s going on around you.” Appropriate for what it offers, the gadget has a quasi-Tamagotchi feel to it — a lightweight, personality-filled device designed to keep users always connected to Meta’s software. It also feels like a relatively low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses. sources.title: Meta open sources code to let you make Muse AI gadgets
passages: Meta now lets you make your own Muse gadgets that feature the company’s new AI agent with code that the company open sourced.
“Muse gadgets are open source devices you build yourself,” Meta says.
With the Muse Home Link, you use community-built skills to have the AI agent “turn on a light, control your TV, send a document to a printer, and more, depending on your setup,” Meta says.

extraction.body: Meta now lets you make your own Muse gadgets that feature the company’s new AI agent with code that the company open sourced. The company suggests projects like loading Muse on a color E Ink display to show reminders, adding it to an HDMI stick so you can display Muse on a big screen, or putting Muse on a small touchscreen device to make what looks kind of like a DIY Muse Charm. “Muse gadgets are open source devices you build yourself,” Meta says. “Program an off-the-shelf ESP32 board or set up a Raspberry Pi with our SDKs, then connect Muse to your displays, buttons, sensors, actuators, and whatever else you’ve got lying on your workbench.” However, Meta cautions that you should “Proceed at your own risk!” The company is also giving away a Muse Home Link gadget that it created. With the Muse Home Link, you use community-built skills to have the AI agent “turn on a light, control your TV, send a document to a printer, and more, depending on your setup,” Meta says.

sources.title: Meta Open-Sources Muse Gadgets: Empower Global Developers to Independently Build Custom AI Peripherals - 36Kr
passages: And just now, Meta has announced a new move: officially launching the Muse Gadgets open source project to fully delegate hardware capabilities, enabling global makers and developers to build exclusive peripheral hardware devices for Muse.
In response to everyone's curiosity about why Meta took the open source move, Alexandr Wang said, "First of all, building all kinds of small gadgets is fun in itself.

According to the information released by Meta, developers can use the ESP32 development board to run the Muse firmware, or use the Linux SDK to connect more complex devices, which means that developers can not only deploy the Muse interaction logic on low-cost microcontrollers, but also directly run the Muse client on more powerful edge computing devices such as Raspberry Pi 5.
For developers who want to get started and try it out, you can follow the steps below to start building your own exclusive Muse peripheral right now:

We believe that Muse is at a special moment, it provides unlimited possibilities for people to create new types of hardware devices, and we are very much looking forward to seeing what kind of works everyone will end up building!"
Meta's route may be exactly this: Muse is responsible for the intelligent capabilities, and developers are responsible for creating various carriers.
In the future, Muse may exist in smartphones, smart glasses, various home devices, and even new hardware created by developers...

At the same time, Meta has also launched an official device: Muse Home Link, a small USB-C powered device, which allows Muse to connect to your home network to communicate with smart home devices, such as TVs, speakers, and any devices that support HTTPS interfaces, further bringing the AI Agent into real life scenarios.

extraction.body: Meta's Muse is still gaining continuous momentum. This newly launched personal AI Agent has already become a key product in Meta's AI strategy this year. Different from traditional chatbots, Muse is designed as an intelligent assistant that can perform tasks on behalf of users: processing emails, shopping, planning itineraries, and even completing a number of complex operations continuously in the background. And just now, Meta has announced a new move: officially launching the Muse Gadgets open source project to fully delegate hardware capabilities, enabling global makers and developers to build exclusive peripheral hardware devices for Muse. According to the information released by Meta, developers can use the ESP32 development board to run the Muse firmware, or use the Linux SDK to connect more complex devices, which means that developers can not only deploy the Muse interaction logic on low-cost microcontrollers, but also directly run the Muse client on more powerful edge computing devices such as Raspberry Pi 5. The official side has also listed a variety of highly practical DIY form references: HDMI Display Stick / Large Screen Expansion: Project the interface or interaction of the Muse Agent directly to a TV or external monitor. Touch-controlled Handheld Pendant: Make a portable interactive terminal similar to Muse Charm, so that you can talk to the Agent at any time without wearing smart glasses. For developers who want to get started and try it out, you can follow the steps below to start building your own exclusive Muse peripheral right now: At the same time, Meta has also launched an official device: Muse Home Link, a small USB-C powered device, which allows Muse to connect to your home network to communicate with smart home devices, such as TVs, speakers, and any devices that support HTTPS interfaces, further bringing the AI Agent into real life scenarios. The official stated that 5000 units of Muse Home Link have been produced in the first trial production run, and shipments are expected to start in a few weeks. While stocks are sufficient, the devices will be distributed directly for free to eligible Muse subscription users for experience. In response to everyone's curiosity about why Meta took the open source move, Alexandr Wang said, "First of all, building all kinds of small gadgets is fun in itself. Secondly, we hope to unlock the creativity of developers and let everyone explore all kinds of brand new, even crazy ideas. We believe that Muse is at a special moment, it provides unlimited possibilities for people to create new types of hardware devices, and we are very much looking forward to seeing what kind of works everyone will end up building!" From this perspective, Meta seems to hope that Muse is not just an official product, but an extensible platform. As soon as the project was released, it immediately attracted the attention of netizens, and even some netizens got started and DIYed their own Muse devices. There are many more user cases like this. Through this attempt of Muse, we can also see a change in the Agent era: In the past, the development path of smart hardware was usually: Company designs hardware — Users purchase devices — Develop applications. But AI Agent may move towards another model: The company provides models and Agent capabilities — Developers create devices of various forms. In fact, starting from AI Pin, the industry has made a lot of explorations in AI hardware, and has tried to replace the mobile phone entry through independent devices, but many products are affected by problems such as functional restrictions and poor interactive experience. Now, manufacturers seem to be changing their minds: directly build a powerful AI Agent first, and then let it enter different hardware. Meta's route may be exactly this: Muse is responsible for the intelligent capabilities, and developers are responsible for creating various carriers. In the future, Muse may exist in smartphones, smart glasses, various home devices, and even new hardware created by developers... So what about you, what do you think of Meta's this attempt? sources.title: Meta Open-Sources Muse AI for Smart Home Revolution
passages: The company announced it's releasing its Muse AI platform as open-source software, giving hardware manufacturers and developers free access to integrate advanced artificial intelligence into consumer gadgets ranging from smart TVs to kitchen appliances.
Muse represents Meta's answer to the fragmented smart home landscape currently dominated by Amazon's Alexa, Google's Assistant, and Apple's HomeKit platforms.

The timing coincides with growing demand for smart home integration, where consumers increasingly expect their devices to understand context and respond intelligently to voice commands and behavioral patterns.
By releasing Muse's source code, the company is essentially handing competitors the keys to build AI-powered devices that could compete directly with Meta's own hardware ambitions.
Early testing has shown Muse can run effectively on processors typically found in mid-range smart TVs and connected appliances, without requiring constant cloud connectivity.
Developers can access Muse through Meta's expanded developer portal, with comprehensive documentation and integration tools available immediately.
The real test will be whether developers embrace Meta's vision quickly enough to establish market leadership before competitors respond with their own open platforms.

extraction.body: Meta just made a bold play for your living room by open-sourcing its Muse AI platform, giving developers free access to integrate artificial intelligence into everything from smart TVs to kitchen appliances. The move signals Meta's shift from closed ecosystems to an open developer strategy that could reshape how AI enters consumer homes. Meta is betting your next toaster will be smarter than your current phone. The company announced it's releasing its Muse AI platform as open-source software, giving hardware manufacturers and developers free access to integrate advanced artificial intelligence into consumer gadgets ranging from smart TVs to kitchen appliances. The announcement represents a dramatic strategic pivot for Meta, which has traditionally kept its AI developments locked within its own ecosystem. By releasing Muse's source code, the company is essentially handing competitors the keys to build AI-powered devices that could compete directly with Meta's own hardware ambitions. "We're seeing the beginning of an AI-everywhere moment," according to industry analysts tracking the consumer electronics space. The timing coincides with growing demand for smart home integration, where consumers increasingly expect their devices to understand context and respond intelligently to voice commands and behavioral patterns. Muse represents Meta's answer to the fragmented smart home landscape currently dominated by Amazon's Alexa, Google's Assistant, and Apple's HomeKit platforms. Rather than building another walled garden, Meta is positioning itself as the underlying intelligence layer that device manufacturers can embed directly into their products. Early testing has shown Muse can run effectively on processors typically found in mid-range smart TVs and connected appliances, without requiring constant cloud connectivity. This open-source strategy mirrors successful developer adoption patterns seen with Google's Android operating system, which gained market dominance by giving manufacturers free access to mobile software. Meta appears to be applying similar logic to the emerging AI-powered device category, betting that widespread adoption will create network effects more valuable than licensing revenue. The implications extend beyond smart homes into automotive, retail, and industrial applications where embedded AI could transform user experiences. coreStoryFacts.text: Appropriate for what it offers, the gadget has a quasi-Tamagotchi feel to it — a lightweight, personality-filled device designed to keep users always connected to Meta’s software.
It also feels like a relatively low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses.
The Muse agent, which is now embodied by a cute digital avatar known within the company as Jolly, lives inside the palm-sized totem that users can carry in their pockets or attach to a keychain.

“We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s keynote. “You just go ahead and tap here in the fingerprint sensor in the corner, and you can start talking without having to unlock a phone or open an app.”
Meta now lets you make your own Muse gadgets that feature the company’s new AI agent with code that the company open sourced.
“Muse gadgets are open source devices you build yourself,” Meta says.
With the Muse Home Link, you use community-built skills to have the AI agent “turn on a light, control your TV, send a document to a printer, and more, depending on your setup,” Meta says.

And just now, Meta has announced a new move: officially launching the Muse Gadgets open source project to fully delegate hardware capabilities, enabling global makers and developers to build exclusive peripheral hardware devices for Muse.
In response to everyone's curiosity about why Meta took the open source move, Alexandr Wang said, "First of all, building all kinds of small gadgets is fun in itself.

According to the information released by Meta, developers can use the ESP32 development board to run the Muse firmware, or use the Linux SDK to connect more complex devices, which means that developers can not only deploy the Muse interaction logic on low-cost microcontrollers, but also directly run the Muse client on more powerful edge computing devices such as Raspberry Pi 5.
For developers who want to get started and try it out, you can follow the steps below to start building your own exclusive Muse peripheral right now:

We believe that Muse is at a special moment, it provides unlimited possibilities for people to create new types of hardware devices, and we are very much looking forward to seeing what kind of works everyone will end up building!"
Meta's route may be exactly this: Muse is responsible for the intelligent capabilities, and developers are responsible for creating various carriers.
In the future, Muse may exist in smartphones, smart glasses, various home devices, and even new hardware created by developers...

At the same time, Meta has also launched an official device: Muse Home Link, a small USB-C powered device, which allows Muse to connect to your home network to communicate with smart home devices, such as TVs, speakers, and any devices that support HTTPS interfaces, further bringing the AI Agent into real life scenarios.

extraction.body: The AI amulet has become a bit of a cliché in the tech industry — devices like Friend have turned the idea of physical AI into little more than an exercise in eye-rolling for many consumers. But that hasn’t stopped Meta from jumping into the arena with its own AI wearable, called Muse Charm, which is designed to give consumers another way to stay connected to its recently launched, and already popular, personal AI agent, Muse. The device, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed in a “one more thing” moment during the company’s annual Connect event, isn’t ready to ship just yet. Zuckerberg said his team had to “finalize laying out the components” and promised the devices would be “ready to ship in time for the holidays in December.” The Muse agent, which is now embodied by a cute digital avatar known within the company as Jolly, lives inside the palm-sized totem that users can carry in their pockets or attach to a keychain. The device comes with a tiny screen that displays the avatar representing the agent. Users can talk to the device, which can then presumably carry out tasks on their behalf. “We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s keynote. “You just go ahead and tap here in the fingerprint sensor in the corner, and you can start talking without having to unlock a phone or open an app.” Zuckerberg added: “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show what’s going on around you.” Appropriate for what it offers, the gadget has a quasi-Tamagotchi feel to it — a lightweight, personality-filled device designed to keep users always connected to Meta’s software. It also feels like a relatively low-stakes way for the social media giant to experiment with AI wearables while also offering yet another way to distribute its AI agent to the masses. sources.title: Meta Open-Sources Muse AI for Smart Home Revolution
passages: The company announced it's releasing its Muse AI platform as open-source software, giving hardware manufacturers and developers free access to integrate advanced artificial intelligence into consumer gadgets ranging from smart TVs to kitchen appliances.
Muse represents Meta's answer to the fragmented smart home landscape currently dominated by Amazon's Alexa, Google's Assistant, and Apple's HomeKit platforms.

The timing coincides with growing demand for smart home integration, where consumers increasingly expect their devices to understand context and respond intelligently to voice commands and behavioral patterns.
By releasing Muse's source code, the company is essentially handing competitors the keys to build AI-powered devices that could compete directly with Meta's own hardware ambitions.
Early testing has shown Muse can run effectively on processors typically found in mid-range smart TVs and connected appliances, without requiring constant cloud connectivity.
Developers can access Muse through Meta's expanded developer portal, with comprehensive documentation and integration tools available immediately.
The real test will be whether developers embrace Meta's vision quickly enough to establish market leadership before competitors respond with their own open platforms.

extraction.body: Meta just made a bold play for your living room by open-sourcing its Muse AI platform, giving developers free access to integrate artificial intelligence into everything from smart TVs to kitchen appliances. The move signals Meta's shift from closed ecosystems to an open developer strategy that could reshape how AI enters consumer homes. Meta is betting your next toaster will be smarter than your current phone. The company announced it's releasing its Muse AI platform as open-source software, giving hardware manufacturers and developers free access to integrate advanced artificial intelligence into consumer gadgets ranging from smart TVs to kitchen appliances. The announcement represents a dramatic strategic pivot for Meta, which has traditionally kept its AI developments locked within its own ecosystem. By releasing Muse's source code, the company is essentially handing competitors the keys to build AI-powered devices that could compete directly with Meta's own hardware ambitions. "We're seeing the beginning of an AI-everywhere moment," according to industry analysts tracking the consumer electronics space. The timing coincides with growing demand for smart home integration, where consumers increasingly expect their devices to understand context and respond intelligently to voice commands and behavioral patterns. Muse represents Meta's answer to the fragmented smart home landscape currently dominated by Amazon's Alexa, Google's Assistant, and Apple's HomeKit platforms. Rather than building another walled garden, Meta is positioning itself as the underlying intelligence layer that device manufacturers can embed directly into their products. Early testing has shown Muse can run effectively on processors typically found in mid-range smart TVs and connected appliances, without requiring constant cloud connectivity. This open-source strategy mirrors successful developer adoption patterns seen with Google's Android operating system, which gained market dominance by giving manufacturers free access to mobile software. Meta appears to be applying similar logic to the emerging AI-powered device category, betting that widespread adoption will create network effects more valuable than licensing revenue. The implications extend beyond smart homes into automotive, retail, and industrial applications where embedded AI could transform user experiences. Major appliance manufacturers including Samsung, LG, and Whirlpool have reportedly begun evaluating Muse integration for next-generation product lines scheduled for 2027 launches. Competitive pressure from OpenAI and other AI companies has accelerated Meta's timeline for developer outreach. The company recognizes that controlling the underlying AI infrastructure could prove more strategically valuable than owning individual device categories in an increasingly fragmented hardware landscape. Developers can access Muse through Meta's expanded developer portal, with comprehensive documentation and integration tools available immediately. Meta's decision to open-source Muse represents a calculated gamble that widespread AI adoption will create more value than proprietary control. If successful, this strategy could position Meta as the invisible intelligence powering millions of everyday devices, fundamentally changing how consumers interact with technology in their homes and beyond. The real test will be whether developers embrace Meta's vision quickly enough to establish market leadership before competitors respond with their own open platforms.

sources.title: Trump expected to name intel chief Clayton as AI czar: reports - france24.com
passages: CBS News reported a day earlier that Clayton was the likely pick and that the administration had discussed keeping him in his intelligence post, with Trump expected to make a final decision shortly.

Washington (United States) (AFP) – President Donald Trump is expected to name Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, as the White House's new AI czar, CNN and other US media reported Friday.
Trump tapped Clayton to lead federal prosecutors in Manhattan at the start of his second term, and the Senate confirmed him as intelligence chief in July.
Trump said last month he would create an "AI Force" modeled on the Space Force he established during his first term, and name a czar to coordinate federal AI efforts.
A longtime Wall Street lawyer, Clayton represented Goldman Sachs during the 2008 financial crisis and Barclays in its purchase of Lehman Brothers' assets.
Trump has resisted tighter AI regulation, arguing a slowdown could hand Chinese firms an advantage and that federal law enforcement can deal with bad actors misusing the technology.
Tech bosses at a White House meeting this week signed a commitment to self-police AI, an accord Trump described as "morally binding."
He chaired the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's first term, where he largely took a pro-business stance but brought enforcement cases against the nascent crypto industry.
Crypto entrepreneurs have since become major Trump backers.

CBS News reported a day earlier that Clayton was the likely pick and that the administration had discussed keeping him in his intelligence post, with Trump expected to make a final decision shortly. A White House official told CBS that any personnel announcement would come directly from the president, dismissing the reports as speculation. Clayton would become the second person to hold the informal title after venture capitalist David Sacks, who held the role at the start of Trump's second term before stepping down. Sacks continues to advise the president on AI, as does Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Trump said last month he would create an "AI Force" modeled on the Space Force he established during his first term, and name a czar to coordinate federal AI efforts. "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he wrote on his Truth Social platform. A longtime Wall Street lawyer, Clayton represented Goldman Sachs during the 2008 financial crisis and Barclays in its purchase of Lehman Brothers' assets. He chaired the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's first term, where he largely took a pro-business stance but brought enforcement cases against the nascent crypto industry. Crypto entrepreneurs have since become major Trump backers. Trump tapped Clayton to lead federal prosecutors in Manhattan at the start of his second term, and the Senate confirmed him as intelligence chief in July. The appointment would come as AI researchers warn of the technology's potential dangers, following cases of AI systems going rogue and hacking outside systems. Trump has resisted tighter AI regulation, arguing a slowdown could hand Chinese firms an advantage and that federal law enforcement can deal with bad actors misusing the technology. Tech bosses at a White House meeting this week signed a commitment to self-police AI, an accord Trump described as "morally binding."

US Sending 3rd Aircraft Carrier, More Troops to Mideast The Pentagon is sending a third aircraft-carrier strike group and an additional Marine expeditionary unit to the Middle East, according to US officials, adding 9,000 to 10,000 more troops to the region as President Donald Trump considers renewing strikes on Iran after the midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported. The ships, jet fighters, Marines and sailors will arrive in the region by the end of November, the officials said. Trump recently told aides that he expects to resume bombing Iran that same month, according to the newspaper. The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt left its home port of San Diego on Sunday on a scheduled deployment, while the USS Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, comprising three amphibious ships carrying Marines from the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit, left on Monday. Two carriers—the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington—are already in the Middle East. If the Washington stays after the Roosevelt arrives it will bring the region to three carrier strike groups for the first time since April, before Iran and the US clinched a fragile ceasefire that temporarily ended fighting that began on Feb. 28. That ceasefire collapsed, and the two sides have fought sporadically since. Besides the Bush and Washington, ships from the USS Boxer Amphibious Ready Group are also in the Middle East. The additional servicemembers on the warships that deployed this week will add to the more than 50,000 troops already in the region, one of the officials said. It is possible that the Washington could leave the region and head back to its home port in Japan, bringing the force back down to two carriers. Spokespeople for the White House and Pentagon didn’t respond to requests for comment. Iran Launches 30 Drone, 10 Missile Attacks Per Week on Ships in Hormuz Iran has been launching dozens of drones and missiles at commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz each week, largely out of the public eye, though it has often failed to strike its targets, confidential data shared with The New York Times by a Western security official who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters shows. Since the beginning of August, Iran has launched about 30 drone attacks and 10 anti-ship missile attacks per week against commercial ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to the data shared with The Times by the official. On Wednesday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corps for the first time appeared to confirm it was behind the near-daily sounds of explosions heard from Iran’s southern coast, saying it was striking targets in the Strait of Hormuz every 24 hours. “We prevent them from passing, but for some time now, America has not responded,” a spokesman for the Revolutionary Guards said in a state news interview. The aggression shows that even as oil exports from the Middle East have rebounded in recent weeks, shipping through the waterway remains risky, as Iran jostles to keep control of one of its biggest sources of leverage. “Negotiations aren’t going anywhere. Neither side is really budging. So it’s a standoff,” said Gregory Brew, an Iran analyst at the Eurasia Group. He said that the violence in the strait “speaks to the position that both sides are in: Neither is looking to aggressively escalate the conflict.” But both, he said, want to control the waterway. Russian Strikes Snarl Traffic on 3 Kyiv Bridges in New Disruption Tactic However, Ukraine has this year made some progress against Russia’s bigger army, according to the Institute for the Study of War. Russian forces lost control over almost 300 square kilometers (116 square miles) between March and September, the Washington-based think tank said in a report late Thursday. Also, it said that the Russian military suffered over 46,000 casualties in September, the highest monthly number this year. It did not say how many Ukrainian troops were killed or wounded. Zelenskyy says sanctions can stop Russian drones and missiles Russia fired more than 100 drones at Ukraine overnight, striking Kyiv and eight other regions, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Almost half of the drones were the jet-powered type that are especially hard to stop, he said. A drone hit a high-rise apartment block in Kyiv, killing one person, he said. At least four people were reported wounded elsewhere. Zelenskyy repeated his appeal for foreign countries to close loopholes in international sanctions on Russia and to add more restrictions on its trade. He said Russia's drones and missiles are “critically dependent” on foreign components. “Every Russian drone can actually be stopped right at the production line,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X. Ukraine has also bombarded Russia with the long-range drones and missiles it now produces, aiming at military manufacturing plants and oil refineries. The Russian Defense Ministry said Friday that its air defenses overnight downed 646 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, occupied Crimea, the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. One person was wounded in Russia’s southwestern Volgograd region, Gov. Andrei Bocharov said. The attack targeted “industrial infrastructure,” The Associated Press quoted him as saying. Ukraine is ready for a truce on energy strikes and the Black Sea Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the partial truce proposals presented to Kyiv by four countries were the first time India has offered to play a role. He repeated Ukraine’s offer of an unconditional ceasefire on the front line. But Moscow has rejected a ceasefire, saying a comprehensive peace deal must be agreed rather than a temporary truce. Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles, Ukraine says Sybiha said Ukraine is requesting some 300 Patriot missiles from partner countries because intelligence services estimate that Russia is holding 600 ballistic missiles in reserve and can produce up to 140 ballistic missiles per month. The US-made Patriot air defense systems can effectively defend against ballistic missiles, which fly fast and drop steeply, but they are in short supply due to the Iran war.

Since the beginning of August, Iran has launched about 30 drone attacks and 10 anti-ship missile attacks per week against commercial ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to the data shared with The Times by the official.

On Wednesday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corps for the first time appeared to confirm it was behind the near-daily sounds of explosions heard from Iran’s southern coast, saying it was striking targets in the Strait of Hormuz every 24 hours.
“We prevent them from passing, but for some time now, America has not responded,” a spokesman for the Revolutionary Guards said in a state news interview.

The aggression shows that even as oil exports from the Middle East have rebounded in recent weeks, shipping through the waterway remains risky, as Iran jostles to keep control of one of its biggest sources of leverage.
“Negotiations aren’t going anywhere. Neither side is really budging. So it’s a standoff,” said Gregory Brew, an Iran analyst at the Eurasia Group.
He said that the violence in the strait “speaks to the position that both sides are in: Neither is looking to aggressively escalate the conflict.” But both, he said, want to control the waterway.
Russian Strikes Snarl Traffic on 3 Kyiv Bridges in New Disruption Tactic
However, Ukraine has this year made some progress against Russia’s bigger army, according to the Institute for the Study of War.

Russian forces lost control over almost 300 square kilometers (116 square miles) between March and September, the Washington-based think tank said in a report late Thursday. Also, it said that the Russian military suffered over 46,000 casualties in September, the highest monthly number this year. It did not say how many Ukrainian troops were killed or wounded.

Zelenskyy says sanctions can stop Russian drones and missiles Russia fired more than 100 drones at Ukraine overnight, striking Kyiv and eight other regions, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Almost half of the drones were the jet-powered type that are especially hard to stop, he said.
A drone hit a high-rise apartment block in Kyiv, killing one person, he said. At least four people were reported wounded elsewhere.

Zelenskyy repeated his appeal for foreign countries to close loopholes in international sanctions on Russia and to add more restrictions on its trade. He said Russia's drones and missiles are “critically dependent” on foreign components.
“Every Russian drone can actually be stopped right at the production line,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
Ukraine has also bombarded Russia with the long-range drones and missiles it now produces, aiming at military manufacturing plants and oil refineries.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Friday that its air defenses overnight downed 646 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, occupied Crimea, the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.
One person was wounded in Russia’s southwestern Volgograd region, Gov. Andrei Bocharov said. The attack targeted “industrial infrastructure,” The Associated Press quoted him as saying.

Ukraine is ready for a truce on energy strikes and the Black Sea Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the partial truce proposals presented to Kyiv by four countries were the first time India has offered to play a role.
He repeated Ukraine’s offer of an unconditional ceasefire on the front line. But Moscow has rejected a ceasefire, saying a comprehensive peace deal must be agreed rather than a temporary truce.

Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles, Ukraine says Sybiha said Ukraine is requesting some 300 Patriot missiles from partner countries because intelligence services estimate that Russia is holding 600 ballistic missiles in reserve and can produce up to 140 ballistic missiles per month.
The US-made Patriot air defense systems can effectively defend against ballistic missiles, which fly fast and drop steeply, but they are in short supply due to the Iran war.

Last month, Trump said he plans to appoint an artificial intelligence adviser, known as an "AI czar," and create an "AI force," though he ⁠gave no details ⁠about either initiative or how they would be implemented.

This is the second time Trump has named an adviser to oversee AI-related decisions across the administration, a position he has ⁠dubbed "AI czar." Venture capitalist David Sacks held the role at the beginning of Trump's second term, before leaving his team.
Trump recently told aides that he expects to resume bombing Iran that same month, according to the newspaper.

Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI and argued that additional regulation is unnecessary even as fears grow among lawmakers in Washington and globally about risks posed by the technology.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is reviewing an issue in updated flight management computer (FMC) software on some Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Two U.S. airlines have told Boeing they will not accept new aircraft carrying the software, and the review comes as Boeing awaits certification of the 737-10. In a statement to Airways, the FAA said it is aware of a potential issue in a software update for the flight computers on certain 737 MAX aircraft and is working closely with Boeing and the airlines. The agency said it "will convene a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern." According to the FAA, a CARB consists of FAA safety experts and is the agency's standard process for determining whether an issue is a safety concern and, if so, how to address it most effectively. Boeing told operators in a bulletin in late August that the glitch is not an immediate safety issue , CBS reported. In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue. The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem. CBS reported that the condition can arise in rare cases when the crew is flying a precision approach with the autopilot engaged, initiates a missed approach, or go-around, and then changes the preprogrammed flight plan. In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week . VNAV follows the vertical profile the FMC computes from the flight plan's altitude and speed constraints. Level change instead holds a target airspeed while the autothrottle sets climb or idle thrust, and vertical speed holds a rate of climb or descent the pilot selects. Neither mode follows the FMC's vertical path, so crews must manage those constraints themselves. CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach. Boeing said the autopilot continues to function if VNAV disengages and that pilots are trained to land without it. The company told CNBC it is "working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur." Boeing told Airways it "anticipates the next software update in 2028" and is working to accelerate that timeline based on operator feedback. CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward. The glitch surfaced in FMC software versions 14 and 14.1, CBS reported. Alaska Airlines (AS), American Airlines (AA), Southwest Airlines (WN), and United Airlines (UA) each told CBS that none of their in-service 737 MAX aircraft use the affected software. Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes." Those statements concern aircraft already in service. For new deliveries, Southwest and United have told Boeing they will not accept delivery of new aircraft with the affected software and would take aircraft with a previous version instead, CBS reported. The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers. CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment. Boeing told Airways it did not have specific aircraft figures to share, so it remains unclear how many undelivered aircraft carry versions 14 or 14.1, or whether any operator outside the U.S. already flies with them. An airline first told Boeing about the condition in November 2024, according to CBS. Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue. Boeing received what a source described to CBS as "additional information from operators" earlier this year, which prompted it to launch a formal safety review board. The Wall Street Journal reported that the formal review began in September, according to an Investing.com summary of the newspaper's report . The board's findings went to the FAA this month and will be reviewed by the CARB. Boeing told Airways that it informed the FAA of the issue as part of its safety review process and is working under the agency's oversight to complete the software update. The FAA certified the 737-7 on August 3. CBS reported that the aircraft was certified with software version 14 and that Southwest, which accounts for nearly all of the type's order book, had been set to begin receiving it this fall; it is unclear whether the airline will take delivery now. CNBC reported it was not immediately clear whether the 737-7 could be delivered or flown with an older software version. The 737-10 used version 14.1 during its certification testing, according to CBS. Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September . Aviation Week reported that it remains unclear whether the software issue will affect the timing of either 737-7 deliveries or 737-10 certification. The FAA's statement did not address either program. Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps." Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more . In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year. He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months." The CARB will review Boeing's safety findings, and the FAA told Airways that the board will also review Boeing's proposed solution. Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review. passages: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is reviewing an issue in updated flight management computer (FMC) software on some Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Two U.S. airlines have told Boeing they will not accept new aircraft carrying the software, and the review comes as Boeing awaits certification of the 737-10.

In a statement to Airways, the FAA said it is aware of a potential issue in a software update for the flight computers on certain 737 MAX aircraft and is working closely with Boeing and the airlines. The agency said it "will convene a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern." According to the FAA, a CARB consists of FAA safety experts and is the agency's standard process for determining whether an issue is a safety concern and, if so, how to address it most effectively.

Boeing told operators in a bulletin in late August that the glitch is not an immediate safety issue , CBS reported. In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue. The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem.

CBS reported that the condition can arise in rare cases when the crew is flying a precision approach with the autopilot engaged, initiates a missed approach, or go-around, and then changes the preprogrammed flight plan. In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week .

VNAV follows the vertical profile the FMC computes from the flight plan's altitude and speed constraints. Level change instead holds a target airspeed while the autothrottle sets climb or idle thrust, and vertical speed holds a rate of climb or descent the pilot selects. Neither mode follows the FMC's vertical path, so crews must manage those constraints themselves. CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach.

Boeing said the autopilot continues to function if VNAV disengages and that pilots are trained to land without it. The company told CNBC it is "working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur." Boeing told Airways it "anticipates the next software update in 2028" and is working to accelerate that timeline based on operator feedback. CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward.

The glitch surfaced in FMC software versions 14 and 14.1, CBS reported. Alaska Airlines (AS), American Airlines (AA), Southwest Airlines (WN), and United Airlines (UA) each told CBS that none of their in-service 737 MAX aircraft use the affected software. Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes."

Those statements concern aircraft already in service. For new deliveries, Southwest and United have told Boeing they will not accept delivery of new aircraft with the affected software and would take aircraft with a previous version instead, CBS reported.

The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers. CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment. Boeing told Airways it did not have specific aircraft figures to share, so it remains unclear how many undelivered aircraft carry versions 14 or 14.1, or whether any operator outside the U.S. already flies with them.
An airline first told Boeing about the condition in November 2024, according to CBS. Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue.

Boeing received what a source described to CBS as "additional information from operators" earlier this year, which prompted it to launch a formal safety review board. The Wall Street Journal reported that the formal review began in September, according to an Investing.com summary of the newspaper's report . The board's findings went to the FAA this month and will be reviewed by the CARB. Boeing told Airways that it informed the FAA of the issue as part of its safety review process and is working under the agency's oversight to complete the software update.

The FAA certified the 737-7 on August 3. CBS reported that the aircraft was certified with software version 14 and that Southwest, which accounts for nearly all of the type's order book, had been set to begin receiving it this fall; it is unclear whether the airline will take delivery now. CNBC reported it was not immediately clear whether the 737-7 could be delivered or flown with an older software version.

The 737-10 used version 14.1 during its certification testing, according to CBS. Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September .

Aviation Week reported that it remains unclear whether the software issue will affect the timing of either 737-7 deliveries or 737-10 certification. The FAA's statement did not address either program. Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps."

Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more . In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year. He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months."
The CARB will review Boeing's safety findings, and the FAA told Airways that the board will also review Boeing's proposed solution.

Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review. The FAA's statement to Airways did not say whether the CARB must conclude before the agency certifies the 737-10.

Following a thorough review, a panel of FAA safety experts on Friday determined a software issue in certain Boeing 737 MAX flight computers is not a safety concern. The FAA’s Corrective Action Review Board made that determination because pilots retain full control of the aircraft and the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous.
As with any situation, the FAA will consider appropriate action if it receives new information about this issue.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is reviewing an issue in updated flight management computer (FMC) software on some Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Two U.S. airlines have told Boeing they will not accept new aircraft carrying the software, and the review comes as Boeing awaits certification of the 737-10. In a statement to Airways, the FAA said it is aware of a potential issue in a software update for the flight computers on certain 737 MAX aircraft and is working closely with Boeing and the airlines. The agency said it "will convene a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern." According to the FAA, a CARB consists of FAA safety experts and is the agency's standard process for determining whether an issue is a safety concern and, if so, how to address it most effectively. Boeing told operators in a bulletin in late August that the glitch is not an immediate safety issue , CBS reported. In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue. The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem. CBS reported that the condition can arise in rare cases when the crew is flying a precision approach with the autopilot engaged, initiates a missed approach, or go-around, and then changes the preprogrammed flight plan. In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week . VNAV follows the vertical profile the FMC computes from the flight plan's altitude and speed constraints. Level change instead holds a target airspeed while the autothrottle sets climb or idle thrust, and vertical speed holds a rate of climb or descent the pilot selects. Neither mode follows the FMC's vertical path, so crews must manage those constraints themselves. CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach. Boeing said the autopilot continues to function if VNAV disengages and that pilots are trained to land without it. The company told CNBC it is "working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur." Boeing told Airways it "anticipates the next software update in 2028" and is working to accelerate that timeline based on operator feedback. CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward. The glitch surfaced in FMC software versions 14 and 14.1, CBS reported. Alaska Airlines (AS), American Airlines (AA), Southwest Airlines (WN), and United Airlines (UA) each told CBS that none of their in-service 737 MAX aircraft use the affected software. Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes." Those statements concern aircraft already in service. For new deliveries, Southwest and United have told Boeing they will not accept delivery of new aircraft with the affected software and would take aircraft with a previous version instead, CBS reported. The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers. CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment. Boeing told Airways it did not have specific aircraft figures to share, so it remains unclear how many undelivered aircraft carry versions 14 or 14.1, or whether any operator outside the U.S. already flies with them. An airline first told Boeing about the condition in November 2024, according to CBS. Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue. Boeing received what a source described to CBS as "additional information from operators" earlier this year, which prompted it to launch a formal safety review board. The Wall Street Journal reported that the formal review began in September, according to an Investing.com summary of the newspaper's report . The board's findings went to the FAA this month and will be reviewed by the CARB. Boeing told Airways that it informed the FAA of the issue as part of its safety review process and is working under the agency's oversight to complete the software update. The FAA certified the 737-7 on August 3. CBS reported that the aircraft was certified with software version 14 and that Southwest, which accounts for nearly all of the type's order book, had been set to begin receiving it this fall; it is unclear whether the airline will take delivery now. CNBC reported it was not immediately clear whether the 737-7 could be delivered or flown with an older software version. The 737-10 used version 14.1 during its certification testing, according to CBS. Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September . Aviation Week reported that it remains unclear whether the software issue will affect the timing of either 737-7 deliveries or 737-10 certification. The FAA's statement did not address either program. Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps." Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more . In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year. He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months." The CARB will review Boeing's safety findings, and the FAA told Airways that the board will also review Boeing's proposed solution. Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review. The FAA's statement to Airways did not say whether the CARB must conclude before the agency certifies the 737-10. Following a thorough review, a panel of FAA safety experts on Friday determined a software issue in certain Boeing 737 MAX flight computers is not a safety concern. The FAA’s Corrective Action Review Board made that determination because pilots retain full control of the aircraft and the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous. As with any situation, the FAA will consider appropriate action if it receives new information about this issue. Copyright © 2026 Airways Publishing LLC. All rights reserved. ‍

Two U.S. airlines have told Boeing they will not accept new aircraft carrying the software, and the review comes as Boeing awaits certification of the 737-10.
Boeing told operators in a bulletin in late August that the glitch is not an immediate safety issue , CBS reported.

In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem.
The FAA's statement did not address either program.
Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps."

Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review.

Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September .
Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more .
In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year.
He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months."
CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward.
The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers.
CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment.
Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes."

In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week .
Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue.

CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach.

sources.title: Apple says it’s tightening macOS ‘Full Disk Access’ controls due to new risks from AI agents - TechCrunch
passages: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS.
The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said.
This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history.
We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote.
The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.
Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.
AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.

As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote. sources.title: Apple Locks Down Mac Disk Access as AI Agents Pose New Risks
passages: Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission.
Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents.
The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer.
The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions.

According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental.

extraction.body: Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission. The move comes weeks after a troubling incident where Meta's Muse AI appeared to access private messages without clear user consent, highlighting how AI tools are pushing the boundaries of data access in ways that weren't anticipated. Apple is slamming the brakes on how deeply apps can dig into Mac file systems, and AI agents are the reason why. The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer. According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental. Just weeks ago, Inc's Jason Aten discovered that Meta's Muse AI chatbot somehow knew the contents of his private messages, despite never explicitly granting the tool permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. The incident, first reported by The Verge, sent ripples through the tech community as it highlighted a troubling gap between user expectations and AI capabilities. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone quickly pushed back, insisting that access to Messages is 'entirely opt-in' and that users must explicitly grant permission. But the controversy exposed how AI agents - sophisticated tools that can autonomously navigate systems and perform tasks - operate in ways that traditional app permission models weren't designed to handle. Unlike conventional software that follows predictable paths, AI agents can dynamically explore file systems, connect disparate data points, and infer information from seemingly unrelated sources. This creates what security experts call 'permission creep' - where an AI tool granted basic access can leverage that foothold to gather far more information than users intended. Apple's response reflects the company's broader privacy-first philosophy, but it also signals recognition that existing security frameworks are struggling to keep pace with AI development. The new controls will likely require apps to implement more granular permission requests, forcing developers to be explicit about what data their AI tools actually need. But it also means greater control over what these increasingly sophisticated tools can access. The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions. Microsoft Windows and various Linux distributions use similar 'administrator' or 'root' access models that could face the same AI-related vulnerabilities. Google's Chrome OS, with its more restrictive app sandbox approach, may prove more resilient, but even Google will need to consider how AI agents interact with cloud-based file systems. Industry observers expect this to be the first of many security updates as companies grapple with AI tools that blur the line between user intent and automated action. As AI agents become more sophisticated and autonomous, the traditional model of granting broad permissions upfront may prove inadequate. Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents. As these tools become more autonomous and capable of connecting data in unexpected ways, traditional permission models are proving inadequate. The real test will be whether other platform makers follow suit quickly enough, and whether developers can build AI tools that are both powerful and respectful of user boundaries. For now, Mac users can expect more security prompts but also more control over their digital privacy.

This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history.
We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote.
The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.
Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.
AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.
Apple will add new limits for “full disk access” on Mac in response to risks posed by AI agents, as reported earlier by TechCrunch.

In an update on Friday, Apple says it’s rolling out new controls to “ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.” The change comes just weeks after Inc’s Jason Aten found that Meta’s Muse AI somehow knew the contents of his messages, despite not giving the chatbot explicit permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac.
Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.
Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission.
Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents.
The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer.
The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions.

According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental.

In an update on Friday, Apple says it’s rolling out new controls to “ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.” The change comes just weeks after Inc’s Jason Aten found that Meta’s Muse AI somehow knew the contents of his messages, despite not giving the chatbot explicit permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. Apple didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

sources.title: Apple Locks Down Mac Disk Access as AI Agents Pose New Risks
passages: Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission.
Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents.
The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer.
The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions.

According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental.

extraction.body: Apple just threw up new security barriers around Mac computers, responding to what the company calls 'substantial' risks from AI agents that can dig through user files without explicit permission. The move comes weeks after a troubling incident where Meta's Muse AI appeared to access private messages without clear user consent, highlighting how AI tools are pushing the boundaries of data access in ways that weren't anticipated. Apple is slamming the brakes on how deeply apps can dig into Mac file systems, and AI agents are the reason why. The company announced Friday it's rolling out new restrictions for 'full disk access' permissions, a powerful capability that lets apps read virtually everything on a user's computer. According to Apple's developer update, the changes aim to 'ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.' The timing isn't coincidental. Just weeks ago, Inc's Jason Aten discovered that Meta's Muse AI chatbot somehow knew the contents of his private messages, despite never explicitly granting the tool permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. The incident, first reported by The Verge, sent ripples through the tech community as it highlighted a troubling gap between user expectations and AI capabilities. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone quickly pushed back, insisting that access to Messages is 'entirely opt-in' and that users must explicitly grant permission. But the controversy exposed how AI agents - sophisticated tools that can autonomously navigate systems and perform tasks - operate in ways that traditional app permission models weren't designed to handle. Unlike conventional software that follows predictable paths, AI agents can dynamically explore file systems, connect disparate data points, and infer information from seemingly unrelated sources. This creates what security experts call 'permission creep' - where an AI tool granted basic access can leverage that foothold to gather far more information than users intended. Apple's response reflects the company's broader privacy-first philosophy, but it also signals recognition that existing security frameworks are struggling to keep pace with AI development. The new controls will likely require apps to implement more granular permission requests, forcing developers to be explicit about what data their AI tools actually need. But it also means greater control over what these increasingly sophisticated tools can access. The challenge extends beyond individual privacy concerns to enterprise environments, where AI agents could potentially access sensitive corporate data through overly broad permissions. Microsoft Windows and various Linux distributions use similar 'administrator' or 'root' access models that could face the same AI-related vulnerabilities. Google's Chrome OS, with its more restrictive app sandbox approach, may prove more resilient, but even Google will need to consider how AI agents interact with cloud-based file systems. Industry observers expect this to be the first of many security updates as companies grapple with AI tools that blur the line between user intent and automated action. As AI agents become more sophisticated and autonomous, the traditional model of granting broad permissions upfront may prove inadequate. Apple's preemptive security move signals a broader industry awakening to the unique risks posed by AI agents. As these tools become more autonomous and capable of connecting data in unexpected ways, traditional permission models are proving inadequate. The real test will be whether other platform makers follow suit quickly enough, and whether developers can build AI tools that are both powerful and respectful of user boundaries. For now, Mac users can expect more security prompts but also more control over their digital privacy.

sources.title: US FAA says Boeing 737 MAX software glitch poses no safety issue - WTVB
passages: WASHINGTON, Oct 2 (Reuters) – The Federal Aviation Administration said on Friday that a panel of experts had determined a software glitch in some Boeing 737 MAX flight computers poses no safety concern, clearing the way ​for approval of a larger version of the best-selling narrow-body jet.
It should also ease concerns at airlines that fly the MAX 7, which uses the same software and was certified by the FAA in August.
Jefferies said in a research note the decision allows the MAX 10 to be certified before the end of the year and estimated Boeing has nearly 1,500 MAX 10s ⁠on order from airlines.

Boeing said it “will continue to follow the lead of the FAA as our ⁠engineers work on the next software update.” Boeing ⁠added it is working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure ​that will allow pilots “to re-enable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur.”

An FAA official said Boeing will issue ​a bulletin to ⁠airlines on how to recognize and respond to the situation should it occur, and the FAA will issue a Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin to US airlines and foreign regulators to ensure they’re aware of Boeing’s bulletin.
